question: Can I sit for another company after I get placed?
answer: A student who receives an offer is considered placed and generally cannot sit for further companies [1]. However, under the dream exception, a placed student may appear for at most one more company if it is in a higher category than the offer already held [1]. A student with a Regular offer may attempt one Standard or one Dream company, while a student with a Standard offer may attempt one Dream company [1]. A student with a Dream offer is out of the process [1]. If the student gets the second offer, the first offer is released and the student must accept the second one [1].

question: How are companies split into Regular, Standard and Dream categories?
answer:
Companies visiting campus are split into three categories based on the cost to company (CTC) they offer [1].
Companies offering a CTC below 6 LPA are classified as Regular [1].
Standard companies offer a CTC from 6 LPA up to but not including 10 LPA [1].
Dream companies offer a CTC of 10 LPA and above [1].
If a company offers a CTC range, the lower figure of the range determines its category [1].

question: What did seniors get asked in the OrbitPay technical interview?
answer: Ritika B. was asked to find the first missing positive number, implement a queue using two stacks, explain how a HashMap works in Java, and write a SQL query with a self-join along with explaining the difference between WHERE and HAVING [1]. She was also asked how to prevent two people updating the same expense from overwriting each other, for which she discussed optimistic locking using row versions [1]. Naveen J. was asked to design an LRU cache, write a SQL query to find accounts whose total debits exceed total credits in the last 30 days, and explain how to prevent double charges on a network timeout and retry using an idempotency key [2]. He was also asked to explain what ACID means using a money-transfer example [2].

sources.title: OrbitPay Fintech interview experience - Ritika B. (ECE, 2026 batch, selected)
sources.text:
Questions: find the first missing positive number, implement a queue using two stacks, and explain how a HashMap works in Java (hashing, buckets, what happens on a collision, and why equals and hashCode must agree). In SQL I was asked the difference between WHERE and HAVING and to write a query with a self join.
About my project he asked: how do you make sure two people updating the same expense do not overwrite each other? I talked about row versions (optimistic locking).

sources.title: OrbitPay Fintech interview experience - Naveen J. (CSE, 2026 batch, selected)
sources.text:
The coding question was to design an LRU cache, which is a hash map plus a doubly linked list. Then SQL: write a query to find accounts whose total debits exceed total credits in the last 30 days.
Then came the part that is specific to a payments company. "A client calls our payment API, the network times out and they retry. How do you make sure the customer is not charged twice?" The answer they want is an idempotency key: the client sends a unique key, and the server stores the result against that key and returns the same result on a retry. He also asked what ACID means with a money-transfer example.

sources.text: The cut-off in the coding test is usually two fully solved problems. There is no service agreement.

sources.title: Veltrix Systems - Software Development Engineer I
sources.text:
1. **Online Coding Test (120 minutes).** Three problems: one easy, one medium and one hard. Typical topics are graphs, dynamic programming and binary search on the answer.
2. **Technical Interview 1 (60 minutes).** Two data structure and algorithm problems solved on a shared editor, with time and space complexity.
3. **Technical Interview 2 (60 minutes).** Object-oriented design of a small system such as a parking lot or a rate limiter, plus DBMS questions on indexing, transactions and normalisation.
4. **Hiring Manager Round (45 minutes).** Project deep-dive, basic system design and behavioural questions.

sources.text: I solved two of the three problems. The hard problem was dynamic programming on intervals and almost nobody finished it, so do not panic if you cannot.

sources.title: Veltrix Systems interview experience - Harini V. (CSE, 2026 batch, selected)
sources.text: Three problems in 120 minutes. Mine were: an easy array question (rotate an array by k), a medium graph question (number of connected groups of warehouses, which is counting components with BFS or union-find), and a hard dynamic programming question on minimum cost to split a delivery route. I solved the first two completely and got partial marks on the third. Two fully solved problems was the cut-off; 14 students went through.

question: What was in the Brightpath take-home assignment?
answer:
The take-home assignment required building a small quiz page in React within 48 hours using a given design file [1][2].
It needed to include a question list, a countdown timer, and a results screen [1][2].

sources.title: Brightpath Edtech interview experience - Isha G. (CSE, 2026 batch, selected)
sources.text:
We got a design file and 48 hours to build a quiz page in React: a question list, a countdown timer and a results screen. I spent the first evening only planning components and state. I kept the quiz state in one reducer and wrote a custom hook for the timer. I also added keyboard navigation and a README explaining my decisions, and the interviewer later said the README is what got me shortlisted.
Things people lost marks for, according to the feedback email: one giant component, no handling for the timer reaching zero, and copying a UI library without understanding it.

sources.title: Brightpath Edtech - Frontend Developer
sources.text:
1. **Take-home Assignment (48 hours).** Build a small quiz page in React from a given design: a list of questions, a timer and a results screen. Code is judged on structure, not on visual polish alone.
2. **Technical Interview (60 minutes).** A review of the assignment code, then JavaScript fundamentals (closures, promises, the event loop), CSS layout with flexbox and grid, and React state and effects.
3. **Culture Round (30 minutes).** A conversation with the product head about how the candidate learns and works in a team.

sources.title: Brightpath Edtech interview experience - Isha G. (CSE, 2026 batch, selected)
sources.text:
- Treat the assignment like real work: small components, clear names, a README.
- Know why your code re-renders.
- There is no aptitude test here, so spend that time on JavaScript fundamentals.

sources.title: Brightpath Edtech interview experience - Isha G. (CSE, 2026 batch, selected)
sources.text:
The first 25 minutes were a code review of my assignment. "Why is this state here and not in the parent?" "What re-renders when the timer ticks?" Then JavaScript: closures with a counter example, the output order of a snippet mixing setTimeout and promises (the event loop question), and the difference between == and ===.
CSS: centre a div both ways, the difference between flexbox and grid, and how to make a layout work on a small phone. React: useEffect dependency arrays, keys in lists, and controlled inputs.

question: What kind of questions come up in the Kairos Cloud Labs technical interview?
answer:
The technical interview features scenario-based questions like determining why a website is slow [1][2]. 
Other questions include what happens when you type a URL in a browser, the differences between TCP and UDP, what a load balancer does, and the difference between a process and a thread [1][2]. 
Candidates are also asked about Linux file permissions and processes [2]. 
AWS questions cover basics such as what EC2, S3, and security groups are [1].

sources.title: Kairos Cloud Labs interview experience - Lakshmi R. (IT, 2026 batch, selected)
sources.text:
All scenario-based. "A customer says their website is slow. What do you check?" I went through it step by step: is it slow for everyone, check DNS, ping and traceroute, then CPU and memory on the server with top, then the application and database logs. The interviewer kept asking "and if that is fine, what next?".
Other questions: what happens when you type a URL in the browser, the difference between TCP and UDP, what a load balancer does, and the difference between a process and a thread. On AWS she asked only basics: what EC2 and S3 are, and what a security group is.

sources.title: Kairos Cloud Labs - Cloud Support Associate
sources.text:
1. **Online Assessment (75 minutes).** Multiple-choice questions on Linux commands, networking (TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP, subnetting) and operating systems, plus one scripting problem in Python or Bash.
2. **Technical Interview (45 minutes).** Troubleshooting scenarios such as "a website is slow, how do you find out why?", Linux file permissions, processes, and what happens when you type a URL into a browser.
3. **Managerial Round (30 minutes).** Handling an angry customer, prioritising tickets, and comfort with shifts.
4. **HR Interview (15 minutes).**

sources.title: Kairos Cloud Labs interview experience - Lakshmi R. (IT, 2026 batch, selected)
sources.text: Mostly multiple-choice questions on Linux and networking. Examples: what does chmod 754 mean, which command shows running processes, what is the default port for HTTPS, and how many hosts are in a /26 subnet. The scripting problem was to read a log file and print the ten most frequent IP addresses. I wrote it in Python with a dictionary.

sources.title: Kairos Cloud Labs interview experience - Lakshmi R. (IT, 2026 batch, selected)
sources.text:
- Use Linux daily for a month before the drive. Commands you have typed are easier to recall than commands you have read.
- Learn subnetting properly.
- In troubleshooting questions, structure matters more than the final answer.

sources.text: A role play where the manager acted as an angry customer whose server was down. Stay calm, repeat the problem back, give a time for the next update. He also asked directly whether I was fine with night shifts one week in four.

question: How long should my answer to 'tell me about yourself' be?
answer: Your answer to "tell me about yourself" should be kept under 90 seconds [1].

sources.title: HR Interview Preparation Guide
sources.text: Keep it under 90 seconds. Start with your branch and college, then one or two projects or an internship that relate to the role, then why you are interested in this role. Do not recite your resume and do not start from your school.

sources.section: Questions you will almost certainly get
sources.text:
1. Tell me about yourself.
2. Why do you want to join this company?
3. What are your strengths and weaknesses?
4. Tell me about a time you worked in a team and something went wrong.
5. Where do you see yourself in five years?
6. Are you willing to relocate or work in shifts?
7. Are you comfortable with the service agreement?

sources.title: HR Interview Preparation Guide
sources.text:
For any "tell me about a time" question, answer in four parts:
- **Situation:** the context, in one sentence.
- **Task:** what you were responsible for.
- **Action:** what you did, in the most detail.
- **Result:** what happened, with a number if you have one.
Prepare four stories in advance: a team conflict, a failure, a time you led something, and a time you learned something quickly. Most behavioural questions can be answered with one of these four.

sources.title: Aptitude Test Preparation Guide
sources.text:
- Most tests give about one minute per question. If a question takes more than 90 seconds, mark it and move on.
- Check whether there is negative marking before you start. If there is none, attempt every question.
- Where there is a sectional cut-off, give each section its planned time even if another section feels easier.
- In data interpretation, read all the questions of a set before calculating. Often two answers come from one calculation.

sources.title: HR Interview Preparation Guide

question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in SQL?
answer: WHERE filters rows before grouping [1]. HAVING filters groups after aggregation [1]. A condition on an aggregate such as COUNT must go in HAVING [1].

sources.title: SQL Preparation Guide
sources.text: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. A condition on an aggregate such as COUNT must go in HAVING.

sources.title: OrbitPay Fintech interview experience - Ritika B. (ECE, 2026 batch, selected)
sources.text:
Questions: find the first missing positive number, implement a queue using two stacks, and explain how a HashMap works in Java (hashing, buckets, what happens on a collision, and why equals and hashCode must agree). In SQL I was asked the difference between WHERE and HAVING and to write a query with a self join.
About my project he asked: how do you make sure two people updating the same expense do not overwrite each other? I talked about row versions (optimistic locking).

sources.title: SQL Preparation Guide
sources.text:
1. SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT and DISTINCT.
2. Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, with GROUP BY and HAVING.
3. Joins: INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL and self joins.
4. Subqueries: in WHERE, in FROM, and correlated subqueries. EXISTS and NOT EXISTS.
5. Window functions: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LAG, LEAD, and running totals with SUM OVER.
6. NULL handling: IS NULL, COALESCE, and how aggregates ignore NULL.
7. Basics of design: primary key, foreign key, normalisation up to 3NF, and indexes.
8. Transactions: ACID properties and isolation levels (for product and fintech companies).

sources.title: SQL Preparation Guide
sources.text:
- Selecting a column that is neither grouped nor aggregated.
- Using INNER JOIN where rows without a match are needed.
- Forgetting that COUNT(column) skips NULL but COUNT(*) does not.
- Comparing with NULL using equals instead of IS NULL.

sources.section: Questions that come up every year
sources.text:
- Second highest salary, overall and per department.
- Employees who earn more than their manager (self join).
- Customers who never placed an order (LEFT JOIN with IS NULL, or NOT EXISTS).
- Top three products by revenue in each category (window function with PARTITION BY).
- Duplicate rows in a table (GROUP BY with HAVING COUNT greater than 1).
- Month-on-month growth (LAG).
- Running total of sales by date.

question: In what order should I study data structures and algorithms?
answer:
You should study the topics in the following order:
1. Arrays and strings [1].
2. Hash maps and sets [1].
3. Linked lists [1].
4. Stacks and queues [1].
5. Binary search [1].
6. Trees [1].
7. Heaps [1].
8. Graphs [1].
9. Dynamic programming [1].

sources.title: Data Structures and Algorithms Preparation Guide
sources.text:
Study in this order. Each topic builds on the previous one.
1. Arrays and strings: two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums.
2. Hash maps and sets: counting, lookups, anagram and duplicate problems.
3. Linked lists: reverse, find the middle, detect a cycle, merge two sorted lists.
4. Stacks and queues: valid parentheses, next greater element, queue using two stacks.
5. Binary search: on sorted arrays and on the answer.
6. Trees: traversals, height, lowest common ancestor, binary search tree checks.
7. Heaps: k-th largest, top k frequent, merge k sorted lists.
8. Graphs: BFS, DFS, connected components, shortest path.
9. Dynamic programming: climbing stairs, knapsack, longest common subsequence, longest increasing subsequence.

sources.title: Data Structures and Algorithms Preparation Guide
sources.text: Almost every software role on campus tests data structures and algorithms in the online test and in at least one interview. Standard category companies mostly ask easy to medium problems on arrays, strings, hash maps and linked lists. Dream category companies add trees, graphs, heaps and dynamic programming.

sources.title: Data Structures and Algorithms Preparation Guide
sources.text: Repeat the problem in your own words, ask about input size and edge cases, state a brute-force idea first, then improve it. Dry-run your code on a small example before saying you are done. Interviewers give credit for a clear approach even when the code is incomplete.

sources.title: Data Structures and Algorithms Preparation Guide
sources.text:
- Solve on paper or in a plain editor at least twice a week. Interviews often have no autocomplete.
- For every problem, write the time and space complexity before you look at any solution.
- Keep an error log: one line per mistake, such as "forgot the empty input case". Read it before every test.
- Re-solve a problem you failed after three days without looking at the solution.

sources.title: Data Structures and Algorithms Preparation Guide
sources.text:
- Memorising solutions instead of patterns.
- Skipping easy problems and then failing them under time pressure.
- Ignoring complexity analysis.
- Practising only in one language feature set and not knowing the standard library for maps, sets and heaps.
